title: The Bay Before 1769
text: Before any European sees it, the bay is ringed by tidal marsh, with oak-dotted grassland behind. About a hundred villages of Ohlone, Miwok, Pomo, Wappo and Patwin people stand along its creeks and shores.
note: [Region] Terrain c.1800 cover (SFEI baylands / historical ecology, decision 12); 105 contact-era villages: data/manual/ohlone/villages.csv (75), early_sf.csv yel_* (5), early_region.csv (25).

title: A Village on Mission Creek
text: The tip of the peninsula, where San Francisco will stand, is home to the Yelamu, a group of 160 to 300 Ohlone people. They move with the seasons between villages of dome-shaped reed houses such as Chutchui, here on Mission Creek.
note: [SF] Map shows: tule houses of early_sf.csv yel_chutchui (1700-1784.4; position approximate, drawn at 2x). population.csv 1769 (Milliken: 160-300).

title: Portolá Sights the Bay
text: November 4, 1769: a Spanish expedition traveling overland under Gaspar de Portolá climbs Sweeney Ridge and looks down on the bay. They are the first Europeans known to see it; ships had always sailed past its narrow, foggy entrance.
note: [Peninsula] events.csv 1769-11-04 Portolá Sights the Bay; places.csv Sweeney Ridge label. "Ships had sailed past the entrance": general knowledge, not in the repo.

title: The First Ship Enters
text: August 5, 1775: the Spanish ship San Carlos, under Juan Manuel de Ayala, sails through the narrow strait later named the Golden Gate. Its crew are the first Europeans known to enter the bay, and they stay until September 18.
note: [SF] events.csv 1775-08-05 Through the Golden Gate; map shows the unbridged strait and landmarks.csv punta_del_cantil_blanco (white cliff, 1700-1853). No ship is drawn.

title: Spain Builds a Fort
text: September 17, 1776: Spain founds a presidio, a small army post, to guard the bay. It is the northernmost outpost of Spain's American empire. The 193 soldiers and settlers build a wooden chapel, a storehouse and thatched huts.
note: [SF] events.csv 1776-09-17 Presidio Founded (northernmost outpost of New Spain); landmarks.csv el_presidio_1776 (1776-1781); population.csv 1776 presidio = 193.

title: Mission Dolores
text: Spanish priests found a mission here on October 9, 1776, to convert the native people and put them to work for it. Its adobe (mud-brick) church, finished in 1791, still stands. At its peak about 1,100 converts live in the rows beside it.
note: [SF] events.csv 1776-10-09 Mission Dolores; landmarks.csv mission_dolores (model built 1782.5-1791.5), quadrangle 1794-95, rancheria rows 1-4 (1793-1798); population.csv 1815 mission_dolores = 1,100.

title: Mission Santa Clara and San José
text: Two more Spanish settlements lie at the south end of the bay. Mission Santa Clara, flooded out of its first site in 1779, stands on its third. San José, founded nearby in 1777 as a farming town, has 171 people in 1800.
note: [South Bay] early_region.csv scl_m1_* (first site 1777-1779.86, flooded Jan 1779), scl_m3_* (third site, church 1781.88-, rancheria rows 1793-1806), sj_pv_houses_1777 (pueblo 1777.91); population_places.csv San Jose 1800 = 171. "Farming town": general knowledge. The pueblo (4.5 km SE) is outside this view.

title: The Russians at Fort Ross
text: 1812: Russia, pushing down the coast from Alaska, plants a colony north of the bay. Ivan Kuskov of the Russian-American Company lands 25 Russians and 80 Alaskans and builds a redwood stockade. The Russians stay until 1841.
note: [North Bay] landmarks_northbay.csv fort_ross_stockade_1812 (model built 1812.2-1812.7), fort_ross_russian_buildings (1812.2-1814.0, end 1842); villages.csv kas_metini. Departure 1841: CLAUDE.md arc / general knowledge.

title: The Ranchos
text: Under Spain and then Mexico, a few families are granted huge cattle ranches called ranchos. Luis María Peralta's Rancho San Antonio, granted in 1820, runs from San Leandro Creek to today's Berkeley. His son Antonio builds this adobe house in 1821.
note: [East Bay] early_region.csv ala_peralta_shelter_1820, ala_peralta_adobe_1821 (1821.8-1897.5; granted to Luis Maria Peralta 1820); other Peralta adobes of the rancho (San Leandro Creek, Temescal, Codornices Creek) in the same table. Open grassland before 1850: decision 13b.

title: Yerba Buena
text: June 1835: William Richardson, an English-born trader, pitches a tent above a sheltered cove where ships anchor. A village called Yerba Buena grows up around him. By 1846 it has about 200 people.
note: [SF] early_sf.csv yb_* (Richardson tent 1835.45, Leese 1836, Casa Grande 1837.5, Custom House 1845.7 ...); events.csv 1835 Yerba Buena Begins; places.csv sf_yerba_buena (1835-1847); population.csv 1846 = 200. "English-born": general knowledge.

title: Vallejo's Rancho
text: North of the bay, the Mexican commander Mariano Vallejo holds a ranch of 66,000 acres. From 1836 he builds this adobe headquarters near Petaluma, the largest private adobe building in California, where hundreds of Native workers raise cattle and grain and tan hides.
note: [North Bay] landmarks_northbay.csv rancho_petaluma_adobe (built 1836-1846: the model rises over the stop). 66,000 acres, largest privately owned adobe, Native labor: the cited Wikipedia page / California State Parks, general knowledge.

title: The Bear Flag Revolt
text: Sonoma is Mexico's northern frontier town, built around the last of California's 21 missions and General Mariano Vallejo's barracks. On June 14, 1846, American settlers seize it, arrest Vallejo, and raise a homemade flag with a bear to declare California independent.
note: [North Bay] landmarks_northbay.csv mission_san_francisco_solano_convento (1832-), _chapel (1841-; 21st and last mission, founded 1823), sonoma_barracks (1841-; Bear Flag Party headquarters June 14, 1846). Arrest of Vallejo, the flag and the declared republic: general knowledge (California Republic), not in the repo.

title: Yerba Buena Becomes San Francisco
text: July 9, 1846: the United States, at war with Mexico, takes California. Sailors from the warship Portsmouth raise the American flag on Yerba Buena's plaza. On January 30, 1847, the village, soon counted at 459 people, is renamed San Francisco.
note: [SF] events.csv 1846-07-09 The Stars and Stripes, 1847-01-30 Yerba Buena Renamed; places.csv sf_yerba_buena -> sf_san_francisco_1847 (the label changes during the stop); population.csv 1847 = 459 (June census); early_sf.csv yb_custom_house on the plaza.

title: Gold!
text: January 24, 1848: gold is found in the Sierra Nevada foothills. That spring Sam Brannan, who owns San Francisco's first newspaper and a store near the mines, runs through these streets shouting “Gold! Gold on the American River!” The town of 800 empties.
note: [SF] events.csv 1848-01-24 Gold!; map shows early_sf.csv yb_stephen_smith_house (Sam Brannan's home and California Star office, 1846-1850) beside the plaza; population.csv 1848 = 812. Brannan's shout, newspaper and store: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11), which gives no exact date ("early in 1848"). "The town empties": general knowledge.

title: An Instant City
text: By the end of 1849 some 25,000 people crowd a town that had 800. Ships abandoned by crews bound for the mines become storehouses. Sand is dumped into the shallow cove, and by 1853 the shore has moved two blocks east, from Montgomery Street to Battery Street.
note: [SF] fill_zones.csv sf_ybc_1_montgomery_sansome (1849-1851.7; storeship Niantic beached at Clay & Sansome 1849), sf_ybc_2_sansome_battery (1850-1853); population.csv 1849.92 = 25,000; OHM gold-rush outlines + sf_extent_1849/1852 fabric. Ships are not drawn.

title: The City Burns
text: The boomtown of wood and canvas burns again and again. On May 4, 1851, fire destroys the heart of the city, including ships used as storehouses. San Francisco rebuilds in brick: the four-story Montgomery Block of 1853 is the tallest building in the West.
note: [SF] Fire-only stop: OHM gold-rush buildings end 1851.34 (Burnt District map of the May 4, 1851 fire, decision 39); fill_zones note: storeships General Harrison and Apollo burned in the May 1851 fire; landmarks.csv montgomery_block (model built 1852.8-1853.9, after this stop). "Again and again": general knowledge (six fires 1849-51).

title: The Mountain Everything Is Measured From
text: July 1851: surveyor Leander Ransom climbs Mount Diablo and marks a starting point on its summit. Property lines across two-thirds of California and all of Nevada are still measured from that spot, which is why so many roads and fences here run exactly north-south.
note: [East Bay] Terrain (Mount Diablo, 3,849 ft); landmarks_eastbay.csv mount_diablo_summit_building stands over the initial point from 1942. Ransom's survey of July 17-18, 1851 and the extent of the Mount Diablo base and meridian: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: Benicia, State Capital
text: California becomes a state in 1850, and its government moves from town to town. From February 3, 1853, to February 24, 1854, the Legislature meets in this brick city hall in Benicia, the third capital, before settling in Sacramento.
note: [Solano-Delta] landmarks_northbay.csv benicia_capitol (1852-; third capitol, Feb 3, 1853 - Feb 24, 1854). Statehood 1850: general knowledge.

title: The Navy Yard at Mare Island
text: September 16, 1854: Commander David Farragut takes charge of a new shipyard on Mare Island, the U.S. Navy's first base on the Pacific coast. Over 142 years the yard builds more than 500 ships, and the city of Vallejo grows up across the channel to serve it.
note: [North Bay] industrial_sites mare_island (1854-1996) with its dated footprints (earliest 1855). Farragut, first Pacific base, 500+ ships built, closed April 1, 1996: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: A Fort at the Golden Gate
text: The U.S. Army spends eight years building a brick fort at the narrowest point of the Golden Gate to guard the entrance to the bay. Finished in 1861, as the Civil War begins, Fort Point never fires a shot in battle. The great bridge will later arch right over it.
note: [SF] landmarks.csv fort_point (built 1853.5-1861: the model rises over the stop). Never fired in anger; the bridge's arch was added to spare it: general knowledge / NPS.

title: Emperor Norton
text: September 17, 1859: Joshua Norton, a merchant ruined by a bad bet on rice, declares himself Emperor of the United States in a newspaper. San Francisco plays along for 20 years. He lives in a rented room on this street, and about 10,000 people view his body in 1880.
note: [SF] Not in the repo tables: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11): proclamation Sept 17, 1859 (Daily Evening Bulletin), rice 1852, room at 624 Commercial St 1865-1880, died Jan 8, 1880, about 10,000 viewed the body. Map shows the 1850s-60s commercial blocks on Commercial St (sf_extent_1856/1863 fabric, procedural on real lots).

title: A Railroad Down the Peninsula
text: January 16, 1864: the first train runs all the way from San Francisco to San José, about 50 miles. Towns grow up around its stations: San Mateo, Redwood City, Menlo Park, Mountain View. Commuters still ride the same line today, under the name Caltrain.
note: [Peninsula] routes.csv rr_sfsj_peninsula (San Bruno - San Jose, 1864-, now Caltrain), rr_sfsj_main_sf (1864); station towns in region_extents snapshots. Opening to San José on January 16, 1864: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The Hayward Earthquake
text: October 21, 1868, 7:53 a.m.: an earthquake on the Hayward Fault, at the foot of the East Bay hills, kills 30 people and wrecks nearly every building in Hayward. Here it destroys the adobe church of Mission San José, built in 1809.
note: [East Bay] landmarks_eastbay.csv mission_san_jose_1809 (model end 1868.81; notes: destroyed Oct 21, 1868 by the Hayward Fault earthquake), mission_san_jose_1869 follows (built 1868.9-1869.8); early_region.csv adobes ending 1868.81. 30 deaths, 7:53 a.m., Hayward damage: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11). The model ends 2.2 days after effect_year.

title: The Delta Is Diked
text: East of the bay, two great rivers meet in a maze of reed marsh called the Delta. In April 1869 a levee closes around Sherman Island, the first Delta island to be completely walled off and drained. More follow within four years, and marsh becomes farmland.
note: [Solano-Delta] fill_zones.csv dl_sherman_island (1868-1869; levee finished April 1869, first peat island leveed completely, Thompson 1957), dl_twitchell_island 1869, dl_brannan_andrus 1871-72, dl_jersey_island 1872-73; data/manual/delta/. Terrain cover only at this zoom.

title: The Railroad Arrives
text: November 8, 1869: the first railroad across the continent, finished that May, reaches the bay. Its trains stop on Oakland's Long Wharf, where ferries take passengers on to San Francisco. Oakland grows from 10,500 people in 1870 to 34,555 in 1880.
note: [East Bay] routes.csv rr_cp_long_wharf (1869-1919; transcontinental terminus from 1869-11-08; fully open 1871-01-16), fy_oakland_pier (1869-1958); fill_zones.csv al_oakland_long_wharf_mole_*; population_places.csv Oakland 1870, 1880. "Finished that May": general knowledge.

title: Golden Gate Park
text: April 4, 1870: San Francisco sets aside 1,017 acres for a park on its empty western side. Three-quarters of the land is bare, shifting sand dunes. Planting starts at the east end and works toward the ocean over the following decades.
note: [SF] events.csv 1870-04-04 Golden Gate Park; landmarks.csv golden_gate_park (1870-); data/research/parks_dates.md (1,017 acres, three-quarters dunes); woods dated east to west (decision 9); dunes.geojson.

title: Blue Jeans
text: May 20, 1873: Levi Strauss, a San Francisco dry-goods merchant, and Jacob Davis, a tailor from Reno, patent work pants with copper rivets at the pocket corners. Blue jeans begin here, in the wholesale district built on the filled cove.
note: [SF] Not in the repo tables: checked on the cited Wikipedia pages (2026-11): U.S. patent 139,121 of May 20, 1873, Jacob Davis a Reno tailor, Strauss a wholesale dry-goods merchant in San Francisco since 1853/54 (1858 directory: 63 & 65 Sacramento St). Exact site of the firm in 1873 not located; map shows the wholesale blocks on the cove fill (fill_zones sf_ybc_3 / sf_ybc_4, 1852-59) at Sacramento and Battery.

title: The First Cable Car
text: San Francisco's hills are too steep for horses to pull streetcars. On August 2, 1873, Andrew Hallidie tests a car that grips a moving steel cable in a slot under Clay Street. Cable cars soon climb the city's hills and open the heights to building.
note: [SF] events.csv 1873-08-02 First Cable Car; routes.csv cc_clay_hill (Clay St, Kearny - Leavenworth, 1873-1942), later lines cc_sutter 1877, cc_california 1878. "Too steep for horses": general knowledge.

title: The Palace Hotel
text: October 2, 1875: the Palace Hotel opens on Market Street with 755 rooms, the largest hotel in the American West. It is built with silver-mining money by the banker William Ralston, who dies five weeks before the opening. Carriages drive straight into its glass-roofed court.
note: [SF] notable_pre1906.csv / landmarks.csv palace_hotel_1875 (1875-1906.29; 755 rooms, 7 storeys, opened Oct 2, 1875). Ralston's death on August 27, 1875: general knowledge.

title: Nob Hill
text: Silver from Nevada's Comstock mines and railroad profits pour into San Francisco, and cable cars make its steepest hill the best address. Mansions go up for Leland Stanford in 1876, Charles Crocker in 1877 and Mark Hopkins in 1878. Only James Flood's, of 1886, will survive 1906.
note: [SF] notable_pre1906.csv stanford_mansion_1876, crocker_mansion_1877, hopkins_mansion_1878, huntington_colton_mansion_1872 (all end 1906), flood_mansion_1886 (survives; after this stop); routes.csv cc_california (1878-); eras.csv Bonanza City (Comstock silver money). Whose fortune came from railroads and whose from silver: general knowledge.

title: Chinatown
text: Chinese immigrants have come since the gold rush to work in mines and on railroads; this is the oldest Chinatown in North America. A riot against them in July 1877 kills four people. In 1882 Congress bars Chinese workers from the country, a ban that lasts until 1943.
note: [SF] places.csv sf_chinatown label (1850-); landmarks.csv old_st_marys (1854-) at California and Grant (then Dupont); Sacramento St / Dupont St fabric. Riot of July 1877 (four killed), Exclusion Act 1882, repeal December 1943, oldest Chinatown in North America: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11), not in the repo. Day of the riot (July 23) from general knowledge.

title: The Valley of Orchards
text: South of the bay, farmers in the Santa Clara Valley switch from wheat to fruit in the 1870s. Orchards spread out from San José, a town of 12,567 in 1880, until they cover the valley floor. Fruit is the valley's main business for the next 70 years.
note: [South Bay] data/manual/landscape/agriculture.geojson + README: scv_san_jose orchards 1872->1890, scv_campbell_los_gatos 1878->95, grain 1852-62 before; population_places.csv San Jose 1880. Terrain cover (orchard pattern, decision 31) at this zoom.

title: A Tower to Light a City
text: December 13, 1881: San José switches on a 237-foot iron tower that straddles its main intersection. Its electric arc lamps are meant to light the whole downtown at once, two years after Edison's light bulb. It never works very well, but it stands until a storm blows it down in 1915.
note: [South Bay] landmarks_southbay.csv san_jose_electric_light_tower (1881-1915; dedicated Dec 13, 1881; 237 ft with the flagpole; blown down Dec 3, 1915).

title: Surfing Comes to America
text: July 19, 1885: three Hawaiian princes, students at a military school in San Mateo, ride boards cut from local redwood on the waves at the mouth of the San Lorenzo River in Santa Cruz. It is the first surfing recorded on the American mainland.
note: [Coast] Terrain: the San Lorenzo River mouth and the beach; Santa Cruz's built-up extent and the 1892 Sanborn tracing (README_santa_cruz.md) show the town behind it. The princes (David Kawananakoa, Edward Keliiahonui, Jonah Kuhio Kalanianaole) on July 19, 1885: general knowledge / Santa Cruz Surfing Museum; not in the repo.

title: Napa Valley Wine
text: Vineyards have spread up the Napa Valley since the 1860s. Greystone Cellars, built in 1888–89 of local volcanic stone, is 400 feet long, a shared cellar where many growers age their wine. Its architect calls it the largest wine cellar in California.
note: [North Bay] landmarks_northbay.csv greystone_cellars (built 1888.0-1889.6; cooperative cellar, 400 x 78 ft, local tufa; George Percy: largest wine cellar in California); agriculture.geojson napa_valley_mid vineyard era 1868->1885.

title: Stanford University
text: Leland Stanford, a railroad builder and former governor, founds a university on his farm in memory of his only son, who died at 15. The cornerstone is laid on May 14, 1887, and the sandstone Inner Quad is ready when classes begin on October 1, 1891.
note: [Peninsula] landmarks_southbay.csv stanford_inner_quad (construction 1887.37-1891.75; cornerstone May 14, 1887, opening Oct 1, 1891). Founder, his son and the farm: general knowledge, not in the repo.

title: An Observatory on a Mountain
text: James Lick, a piano maker who grew rich on San Francisco land, leaves his fortune to build the most powerful telescope in the world. Lick Observatory opens in 1888 on Mount Hamilton, the first observatory built on a mountaintop and staffed year-round. Lick is buried beneath the telescope.
note: [South Bay] landmarks_southbay.csv lick_observatory (built 1880-1888; 36-inch refractor, then the largest in the world, first light Jan 3, 1888; Lick buried under it 1887). First permanently occupied mountaintop observatory: the cited Wikipedia page.

title: Victorian Row Houses
text: As the city spreads west, builders fill whole blocks with wooden row houses with bay windows and carved trim, the style now called Victorian. The houses here are drawn from fire-insurance maps of 1899. The seven “Painted Ladies” on Steiner Street go up in 1892–96.
note: [SF] landmarks.csv painted_ladies (built 1892-96, Matthew Kavanaugh), alamo_square; Sanborn tracing of the Western Addition 1899 + 1913 (decision 27; 6,057 traced footprints).

title: The Midwinter Fair
text: January 27, 1894: hoping to pull the city out of a depression, newspaper publisher M. H. de Young opens a world's fair in Golden Gate Park. It draws more than two million visits in five months and leaves behind the Japanese Tea Garden, the Music Concourse and a museum.
note: [SF] landmarks.csv midwinter_fair_1894, midwinter_fair_electric_tower (1894-96), de_young_museum_1895 (the fair's Fine Arts Building, -1929), japanese_tea_garden, music_concourse (1894-). Attendance (over two million): the cited Wikipedia page, rounded.

title: The Cliff House and Sutro Baths
text: Adolph Sutro, made rich by Nevada silver, owns the city's ocean edge. When the first Cliff House restaurant burns on Christmas Day 1894, he replaces it with a seven-story castle. Beside it, in 1896, he opens the Sutro Baths: swimming pools under glass.
note: [SF] landmarks.csv cliff_house_1863 (model end 1894.98), cliff_house_1896 (built 1895.6-1896.2), sutro_baths (built 1894.3-1896.2, opened March 14, 1896), sutro_heights_mansion. Sutro's biography and the glass roof: general knowledge.

title: The Ferry Building
text: No bridge crosses the bay, so almost everyone arrives by boat. On July 13, 1898, the Ferry Building opens at the foot of Market Street with a 245-foot clock tower. Ferries from Oakland, Alameda and Sausalito land here.
note: [SF] events.csv 1898-07-13 Ferry Building Opens; landmarks.csv ferry_building (model built 1896.0-1898.53, tower 245 ft); routes.csv fy_oakland_pier, fy_alameda_pier, fy_sausalito, fy_creek_route.

title: The Crookedest Railroad in the World
text: August 22, 1896: a steam railway opens from Mill Valley to the top of Mount Tamalpais, twisting through 281 curves in eight miles. Day-trippers ride up for the view and coast back down in open gravity cars. Automobiles and a 1929 fire put it out of business in 1930.
note: [North Bay] data/manual/ohm historic_rail (Mt Tamalpais & Muir Woods Railway, decision 39), routes.csv. Opening date, 281 curves, 8.19 miles, closure in 1930: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The House That Never Stopped Growing
text: Since 1886 Sarah Winchester, heir to the Winchester rifle fortune, has kept carpenters adding to her farmhouse near San José. By now it is a maze of about 160 rooms with a seven-story tower. The 1906 earthquake will bring the tower down; the building goes on until she dies in 1922.
note: [South Bay] landmarks_southbay.csv winchester_mystery_house (bought 1886, 160 rooms at her death in 1922) and winchester_tower_1906 (seven-storey tower, built 1895-1900, fell April 18, 1906; position and years LOW CONFIDENCE in the model).

title: Saving the Redwoods
text: Loggers have cut most of the ancient redwoods of the Santa Cruz Mountains to build the cities around the bay. In 1902, after a campaign led by the photographer Andrew Hill, the state buys a surviving grove at Big Basin. It becomes California's first state park.
note: [Coast] Terrain: logged redwood country is brush until its second growth (decision 41), the old-growth basin stays forest. Park established 1902 (California Redwood Park), Andrew P. Hill and the Sempervirens Club: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The Key System
text: October 26, 1903: electric trains begin running from Berkeley out along a three-mile pier into the bay, where ferries carry riders on to San Francisco. Their builder, Francis "Borax" Smith, also sells the land along the lines, and the East Bay's streetcar suburbs fill with houses.
note: [East Bay] routes.csv ks_mole (Key System mole and pier, 1903-1939), ks_trunk, ks_f_berkeley (1903-1958). First train October 26, 1903; Smith's Realty Syndicate: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The City in 1905
text: San Francisco is the largest city on the West Coast, with 342,782 people in 1900. Newspaper towers line Market Street; the 315-foot Call Building is the tallest west of Chicago. The domed City Hall of 1899 took nearly three decades to build.
note: [SF] landmarks.csv call_building_1898 (315 ft, tallest west of Chicago), city_hall_1899 (construction 1870/71-1899; position approximate, LOW CONFIDENCE model); notable_pre1906.csv chronicle_building_1890, hearst_building_1898; population.csv 1900. "Largest city on the West Coast": general knowledge.

title: April 18, 1906
text: At 5:12 a.m. a magnitude 7.9 earthquake strikes. The fires that follow do far more damage: they burn until April 21 and destroy about 28,000 buildings, nearly everything from the waterfront to Van Ness Avenue.
note: [SF] events.csv 1906-04-18 The Great Earthquake (magnitude 7.9, 5:12 a.m.); data/manual/fire_1906_boundary.csv; ~15,700 predecessor buildings end at 1906.29; 28,000 buildings: CLAUDE.md pitfall 1.

title: Santa Rosa, 1906
text: The same earthquake wrecks towns up and down the coast. Santa Rosa, a town of 6,673 people 50 miles north of San Francisco, loses its entire downtown to the shaking and the fire that follows. About a hundred people die there.
note: [North Bay] data/manual/fires/quake_1906_santa_rosa.geojson (outline ESTIMATED, 1906.29; the entire downtown, about a hundred dead); Sanborn tracings of downtown Santa Rosa 1904 / 1908 end at the quake; population_places.csv Santa Rosa 1900 = 6,673. DATA PROBLEM: notable_demolished_region.csv sr_sonoma_county_courthouse_1884 has end_year 1906 (whole year), so the courthouse leaves the map at 1906.0, before the quake.

title: Where the Fire Stopped
text: After three days the fire is stopped at wide Van Ness Avenue and, in the Mission District, at Dolores Street and 20th Street. Just west of Dolores the mission church of 1791 survives. This is why the western half of the city still has wooden houses older than 1906.
note: [SF] data/manual/fire_1906_README.md (lines held at Van Ness, Dolores, 20th St); landmarks.csv mission_dolores (1791-9999); CLAUDE.md pitfall 1 (pre-1906 Victorians survive west of the fire line).

title: The City Rebuilds
text: San Francisco rebuilds on the same streets, and quickly. The ruins are cleared, new office buildings rise downtown, and the Palace Hotel reopens in December 1909. By 1910 the city counts 416,912 people.
note: [SF] sf_buildings in the burned core (136 of today's buildings by 1907, 798 by 1910, 997 by 1912) + sf_rebuild_procedural predecessors; landmarks.csv palace_hotel_1909 (built 1906.55-1909.97); population.csv 1910.

title: Muir Woods
text: One canyon of ancient redwoods near the bay has escaped the loggers. To stop a plan to dam it, businessman William Kent buys the canyon and gives it to the nation. On January 9, 1908, President Theodore Roosevelt makes it a national monument, named for the naturalist John Muir.
note: [North Bay] Terrain: redwood forest in Redwood Canyon. Kent's purchase (1905) and gift, Roosevelt's proclamation of January 9, 1908: general knowledge / NPS.

title: Angel Island
text: January 21, 1910: an immigration station opens in this cove on Angel Island. For 30 years it screens people arriving across the Pacific, most from China and Japan. Because the law bars most Chinese, many are held here for weeks or months; some carve poems into the walls.
note: [Marin] Not in the repo tables: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11): opened Jan 21, 1910, closed 1940, about 175,000 Chinese and 117,000 Japanese, detention from days to 22 months, 200+ poems. Map shows the island and cove (places.csv mar_angel_island) and Fort McDowell (industrial_sites fort_mcdowell, 1900-). DATA PROBLEM: the 11 footprints at the station (China Cove) carry years 1975-1995, so the cove is empty in 1910.

title: Oakland Grows Up
text: Oakland more than doubles in ten years, to 150,174 people in 1910. Electric trains of the Key System carry commuters to a ferry pier three miles out in the bay. In 1910–14 the city builds a 320-foot City Hall, the first skyscraper city hall in the country.
note: [East Bay] landmarks_eastbay.csv oakland_city_hall (built 1910.6-1914.5; 320 ft, first high-rise city hall in the U.S.); routes.csv ks_mole (1903-1939, ~16,000 ft), ks_* lines; population_places.csv Oakland 1900 = 66,960, 1910 = 150,174; Sanborn tracing of downtown Oakland 1912.

title: A World's Fair on New Land
text: To show it has recovered, San Francisco hosts a world's fair for the opening of the Panama Canal. From April 1912 sand is pumped into a shallow cove to make the fairground. The fair opens on February 20, 1915, around the 435-foot Tower of Jewels.
note: [SF] fill_zones.csv sf_marina_cove_1912 (1912.28-1912.7); events.csv 1915-02-20 Panama-Pacific Exposition (636 acres); landmarks.csv ppie_* (30 models; Tower of Jewels 435 ft, built 1914.0-1915.13), palace_of_fine_arts_1915. Panama Canal as the occasion: general knowledge. The camera point is bay until the 1912 fill.

title: Electronics Begins in Palo Alto
text: Decades before Silicon Valley, a radio company called Federal Telegraph sets up in Palo Alto with Stanford graduates. In its Emerson Street laboratory in 1912, Lee de Forest's team finds that a vacuum tube can amplify signals: the discovery behind radio, long-distance telephones and early computers.
note: [Peninsula] Palo Alto Sanborn tracings 1901/1904/1908 (decision 28) show the blocks round Emerson St and Channing Ave. Federal Telegraph (founded 1909), the 1912 amplifier work at 913 Emerson St (California Historical Landmark 836): general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The University at Berkeley
text: The University of California, the state's public university, gets a grand campus in Berkeley: Sather Gate in 1910, Doe Library in 1911 and, in 1915, Sather Tower, a 307-foot bell tower modeled on the one in St. Mark's Square in Venice.
note: [East Bay] landmarks_eastbay.csv sather_gate (1910), doe_library_1911, sather_tower (built 1913.0-1915.0; 307 ft, after St Mark's Campanile).

title: A New City Hall
text: The old City Hall, which took nearly three decades to build, was wrecked in 1906. Its replacement goes up in under three years, starting April 5, 1913, as the centerpiece of a new Civic Center. Its dome is 307 feet high.
note: [SF] landmarks.csv city_hall_1915 (model built 1913.26-1915.95, dome 307.5 ft), civic_auditorium (1915), city_hall_1899 (-1906); places.csv Civic Center (1912-).

title: Hollywood Before Hollywood
text: From 1912 to 1916 the Essanay company makes hundreds of silent movies in the railroad town of Niles, now part of Fremont, filming Westerns in the canyon behind it. In 1915 Charlie Chaplin shoots "The Tramp" here, before the movie business settles in Los Angeles.
note: [East Bay] Region buildings of Niles (50 standing in 1915 round Niles Blvd; years from the rolls). Essanay's Niles studio 1912-16, Chaplin's five 1915 films incl. The Tramp (released April 11, 1915): general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: A Tunnel to the West Side
text: In 1912 San Francisco starts the first big city-owned streetcar system in the country, the Municipal Railway. On February 3, 1918, it opens a two-mile tunnel under Twin Peaks, and the empty sand dunes on the city's west side begin to fill with houses.
note: [SF] landmarks.csv twin_peaks_tunnel (1918), routes.csv Muni lines; buildings of West Portal and the Sunset by their years. Muni's first line December 28, 1912; tunnel 2.27 miles, opened February 3, 1918: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: From Fairground to the Marina
text: The fair's palaces were plaster and wood, built to last a year; all but one are torn down in 1916. The Palace of Fine Arts is spared. During the 1920s houses and apartments cover the rest of the filled cove, which becomes the Marina District.
note: [SF] landmarks.csv ppie_* end 1916, palace_of_fine_arts_1915 (wood and plaster, kept, -1964); sf_buildings in the Marina: 689 before 1920, 1,137 before 1925, 2,303 before 1930; places.csv Marina District (1916-).

title: Berkeley Burns
text: September 17, 1923: a grass fire in the hills, driven by a hot, dry wind, sweeps down into north Berkeley. In two hours it destroys 584 buildings, most of them wood-shingled homes, and stops at the edge of the university campus only when the wind turns.
note: [East Bay] Berkeley 1911 Sanborn tracing + the 1923 fire as a dated clearance (decision 28): buildings ending 1923.71 burn on screen (time-extension DISASTERS). 584 buildings: the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The Santa Cruz Boardwalk
text: Santa Cruz, on the ocean south of the bay, is the region's beach resort. Beside the casino and indoor pool of 1907, the Giant Dipper opens on May 17, 1924: a wooden roller coaster with half a mile of track. It is still running a century later.
note: [Santa Cruz] landmarks_coastsouth.csv giant_dipper_santa_cruz (construction 1924.25-1924.38; 2,640 ft of track; end 9999), boardwalk_casino (1907), boardwalk_plunge (1907).

title: The First Big Bridge
text: Cars are remaking the region, but drivers still cross the water on ferries. On May 21, 1927, the Carquinez Bridge opens across the strait where the Central Valley's rivers enter the bay, putting the bay cities on a direct road to Sacramento.
note: [Solano-Delta] landmarks_northbay.csv carquinez_bridge_1927 (model built 1923.3-1927.39; dedicated May 21, 1927; two 1,100 ft main spans; direct road to Sacramento); routes.csv br_carquinez_1927, auto ferries fy_*. Camera point over the strait (bridge).

title: The Porters of West Oakland
text: Oakland's 16th Street Station is the end of the line for trains from the East. Many of the Black porters who staff the sleeping cars settle nearby in West Oakland. Led here by C. L. Dellums, they join the first Black-led union to win a contract from a major American company, in 1937.
note: [East Bay] landmarks_eastbay.csv sp_16th_street_station (1912); West Oakland Sanborn tracings 1912/1951. Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters (founded August 25, 1925), C. L. Dellums in Oakland, Pullman contract of 1937: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: An Airport on the Marsh
text: May 7, 1927: San Francisco opens an airport, Mills Field, on 150 acres of leased cow pasture, once tidal marsh. In the following decades fill carries its runways far out over the tidal flats, and it becomes San Francisco International Airport.
note: [Peninsula] airports.csv San Francisco International Airport (dedicated May 7, 1927); fill_zones.csv sm_sfo_mills_pasture_field (150-acre lease), sm_sfo_tidelands_1930s (1930.5-1935), later sm_sfo_* phases to 1968.

title: Television Is Invented
text: September 7, 1927: in a rented loft at 202 Green Street, 21-year-old Philo Farnsworth sends a picture of a straight line from one room to the next using no moving parts. It is the first all-electronic television image, the approach that every later TV set builds on.
note: [SF] SF buildings at Green and Sansome Streets (the block stands from 1914-15). Farnsworth's first electronic image on September 7, 1927 at 202 Green St (California Historical Landmark 941): general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: Atom Smashers at Berkeley
text: In 1931 the Berkeley physicist Ernest Lawrence builds the first cyclotron, a machine that whirls particles to enormous speeds to break atoms apart. His laboratory makes the university a world center of physics. In 1941 chemists here discover plutonium, soon used in the atomic bomb.
note: [East Bay] UC Berkeley campus buildings (known_building_dates_region.csv; Gilman Hall, where plutonium was identified on February 23, 1941, stands from 1917). Lawrence's cyclotron (1931) and Nobel Prize (1939): general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: A Hangar for Airships
text: The Navy builds a base at Sunnyvale for its airship USS Macon, a flying aircraft carrier longer than two football fields. Hangar One, built in 1931–33 to house it, is 1,133 feet long and 198 feet high. The Macon is lost at sea in 1935.
note: [South Bay] landmarks_southbay.csv hangar_one_1933 (construction 1931.8-1933.6; 1,133 x 308 ft, 198 ft high; built for USS Macon); airports.csv Moffett Federal Airfield (1933). Macon's size, role and loss in 1935: general knowledge, not in the repo.

title: Coit Tower
text: Lillie Hitchcock Coit, who as a girl was the mascot of a volunteer fire company, leaves a third of her fortune to beautify San Francisco. It pays for this 210-foot tower on Telegraph Hill, finished in 1933. Inside, artists hired by the government paint scenes of California at work.
note: [SF] landmarks.csv coit_tower (built 1932.5-1933.77: rises over the stop; 210 ft). Coit's bequest; murals of the Public Works of Art Project, 1934: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The Bay Bridge
text: In the depths of the Great Depression the region builds two great bridges at once. Work on the first starts July 9, 1933. It opens November 12, 1936: two suspension spans to Yerba Buena Island, a tunnel through it, and steel trusses on to Oakland.
note: [SF] events.csv 1936-11-12 Bay Bridge Opens; landmark models bay_bridge_west_span and east 1936 spans (built 1933.52-1936.87); routes.csv fwy_i80_bay_bridge. Camera point = centre anchorage, over water (bridge).

title: Bloody Thursday
text: Dockworkers along the West Coast have been on strike since May 9, 1934. On July 5 police open fire near Mission and Steuart streets, killing two men. In answer about 150,000 workers shut down San Francisco for four days; the strike ends with the ports unionized.
note: [SF] Not in the repo tables: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11): strike from May 9, 1934; July 5 shootings near Steuart and Mission (Howard Sperry, Nick Bordoise); general strike July 16-19, about 150,000 workers; unionization of all West Coast ports. Map shows the Embarcadero piers (notable_demolished.csv pier_22_1916, pier_24_1915 ...), the Ferry Building and the Bay Bridge under construction.

title: Alcatraz
text: August 11, 1934: the old Army prison on Alcatraz Island reopens as a federal penitentiary for inmates considered too dangerous for other prisons, the gangster Al Capone among them. It holds prisoners until 1963.
note: [SF] events.csv 1934-08-11 Alcatraz Penitentiary (closes 1963); landmarks.csv alcatraz_cellhouse (Army cellhouse 1909.5-1912), alcatraz_lighthouse_1909. Al Capone and "too dangerous for other prisons": general knowledge.

title: Water from the Mountains
text: October 1934: after 20 years of work, water from the dammed Hetch Hetchy Valley in Yosemite National Park arrives through a 167-mile aqueduct that ends here at Crystal Springs Reservoir. It still supplies San Francisco and its neighbors, about 2.6 million people.
note: [Peninsula] Map shows Upper / Lower Crystal Springs Reservoir (water_history.csv, 1877 / 1888). Not in the repo tables: checked on the cited Wikipedia pages (2026-11): work from 1914, first water October 1934 (infobox Oct 24; celebration Oct 28), 167 miles, 2.6 million people; Pulgas Water Temple at the terminus (37.4833, -122.3171), water flowing into Upper Crystal Springs Reservoir. "In Yosemite National Park": general knowledge.

title: The Golden Gate Bridge
text: The last gap is the Golden Gate itself. Work begins January 5, 1933, and the bridge opens to walkers on May 27, 1937. Its main span of 4,200 feet is the longest in the world until 1964, and its towers stand 746 feet above the water.
note: [SF] events.csv 1937-05-27 Golden Gate Bridge Opens; landmarks.csv golden_gate_bridge (model built 1933.01-1937.4; towers 746 ft). Main span 4,200 ft, longest until 1964: checked on Wikipedia Golden_Gate_Bridge (2026-11). Camera point = mid-span (bridge).

title: The China Clipper
text: November 22, 1935: a Pan American flying boat, the China Clipper, takes off from Alameda with the first airmail to cross the Pacific. It passes under the cables of the unfinished Bay Bridge and reaches Manila a week later, after stops at Hawaii, Midway, Wake and Guam.
note: [East Bay] Ground: fill_zones.csv al_* (Alameda Airport / Benton Field fill at the island's west end, decision 30); landmarks city.ts Bay Bridge under construction (1933-36). The flight of November 22-29, 1935: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page. No building of the Pan Am base is in the data.

title: Treasure Island
text: To celebrate its new bridges the region holds another world's fair, and builds an island for it. From February 1936 Army engineers pile 400 acres of sand on a shoal beside Yerba Buena Island. The fair opens on February 18, 1939.
note: [SF] fill_zones.csv sf_treasure_island (1936.1-1937.65; begun Feb 11, 1936, ~400 acres); events.csv 1939-02-18 Treasure Island Fair; landmarks.csv ggie_* (10 models), treasure_island_building_1 (1938; planned airport terminal). The camera point is water until the fill reaches it c.1936.8 (the fill is the subject).

title: A Garage in Palo Alto
text: In 1938 two Stanford engineers, Bill Hewlett and David Packard, start building electronic instruments in the garage behind this house with $538. Walt Disney's studio buys eight of their first product. The garage is now called the birthplace of Silicon Valley.
note: [South Bay] Not in the repo tables: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11): 367 Addison Ave, Palo Alto (37.4431, -122.1547); garage used from 1938 with $538; partnership 1939; eight HP 200A oscillators to Walt Disney Studios; California Historical Landmark 976, "Birthplace of Silicon Valley". Map shows the houses of the block (92 footprints dated 1884-, Palo Alto Sanborn area).

title: The Wartime Shipyards
text: The United States enters World War II in December 1941, and the Bay Area becomes a shipyard for the Pacific war. At Richmond, Henry Kaiser's four yards launch 747 ships. Workers pour in, many of them women, and the city grows from 23,642 people to 99,545.
note: [East Bay] industrial_sites kaiser_yards_1_2 (1941-1946), kaiser_yard3 (1942-); fill_zones.csv cc_richmond_shipyards (Yard 1 begun Dec 1940); landmarks_ports.csv kaiser_yard3_whirley_cranes (747 ships, NPS); population_places.csv Richmond 1940, 1950. Women workers ("Rosie the Riveter"): general knowledge / NPS park theme.

title: The Doolittle Raid Sails
text: April 2, 1942: four months after Pearl Harbor, the aircraft carrier USS Hornet leaves the new naval air station at Alameda with 16 Army bombers lashed to its deck. Sixteen days later, led by Jimmy Doolittle, they bomb Tokyo, America's first strike on Japan itself.
note: [East Bay] NAS Alameda: airports_extra pavement phased 1941 / 1957 and the Navy fill (decision 30). The carrier piers are where the museum ship USS Hornet (CV-12, a later ship of the same name; landmarks_eastbay.csv, 1998-) is moored. The raid (Hornet CV-8 sailed April 2, bombed Tokyo April 18, 1942): general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: Tanforan
text: After Japan attacks Pearl Harbor, the government orders everyone of Japanese ancestry off the West Coast, citizens included. From April 28, 1942, nearly 8,000 people from the Bay Area are held at this racetrack, many in horse stalls, then sent to a camp in Utah.
note: [Peninsula] Map shows the racetrack: vanished_sites tanforan (1899.84-1964.2, traced on the 1947 USGS sheet); places.csv Japantown (Nihonjin-machi) label ends 1942. Not in the repo tables: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11): April 28 - October 13, 1942; peak 7,816; horse stalls; most sent to Topaz, Utah.

title: Marinship
text: In 1942 a shipyard goes up in three months on the mudflats of Sausalito. Its 20,000 workers launch 93 cargo ships and tankers by 1945. Black workers, shut out of full union membership, sue, and in 1944 California's highest court rules that a union cannot do that.
note: [North Bay] industrial_sites marinship (1942-) and its 17 vanished buildings traced from the 1947 San Francisco North sheet (vanished_buildings.geojson, decision 44). 93 ships, 20,000 workers, James v. Marinship (1944): general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: Port Chicago
text: July 17, 1944: ammunition being loaded onto a ship at this Navy pier explodes, killing 320 men, most of them Black sailors. When 258 survivors refuse to load more, 50 are convicted of mutiny. The case helps push the Navy to end racial segregation in 1946.
note: [East Bay] Map shows the Navy site and the town: industrial_sites concord_nws (Naval Magazine Port Chicago, 1942-), places.csv cc_port_chicago town label (1931-1969). Not in the repo tables: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11): 10:18 p.m., 320 killed (202 African American), 258 refused, 50 convicted, desegregation from February 1946. No explosion effect is drawn.

title: The United Nations Is Born
text: As World War II ends, delegates from 50 nations meet in San Francisco to create an organization meant to keep the peace. On June 26, 1945, they sign the United Nations Charter here in the Veterans Building, facing City Hall.
note: [SF] events.csv 1945-06-26 UN Charter Signed (50 Allied nations, Veterans Building); landmarks.csv war_memorial_veterans_building (1932-), war_memorial_opera_house, city_hall_1915.

title: A Secret Cargo
text: July 16, 1945: hours after the first atomic bomb is tested in New Mexico, the cruiser USS Indianapolis leaves Hunters Point Naval Shipyard carrying the uranium and key parts of the bomb meant for Hiroshima. It delivers them to a Pacific island and, four days after that, is sunk by a Japanese submarine.
note: [SF] landmarks_ports.csv hunters_point_drydock_2/3/4 (1903, 1918, 1943); shipyard buildings and fill by their years. Indianapolis sailed July 16, delivered at Tinian July 26, sunk July 30, 1945: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The Sunset Fills In
text: The western third of San Francisco was sand dunes. Since the 1920s builders have covered them with rows of stucco houses, and after the war the last blocks fill in. In 1950 the city reaches 775,357 people, a number it will not see again until 2000.
note: [SF] sf_buildings (assessor years) in the Sunset: 4,304 footprints before 1925, 14,756 before 1940, 25,910 before 1950 of 30,602; dunes.geojson; population.csv 1950 = 775,357, 1990 = 723,959, 2000 = 776,733.

title: Saving the Cable Cars
text: In 1947 the mayor proposes replacing the cable cars with buses. Friedel Klussmann and a committee of women's civic groups force a public vote, and San Franciscans choose to keep the Powell Street lines by 166,989 votes to 51,457.
note: [SF] Map shows the surviving lines: routes.csv cc_powell_mason (1888-9999), cc_california (1878-9999), cc_powell_hyde (1957-). Not in the repo tables: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11): 1947 proposal by Mayor Lapham, 27 women's civic groups, 166,989 yes to 51,457 no. Vote dated November 1947 from general knowledge (stop year 1947.84).

title: Orchards to Suburbs
text: After the war families pour into California, and the Santa Clara Valley's orchards, some 100,000 acres at their peak, are cut down for housing tracts. San José grows from 95,280 people in 1950 to 459,913 in 1970.
note: [South Bay] agriculture.geojson topo_1940s orchards (real, USGS 1939-56) ending as cells become city; region footprints Sunnyvale - Santa Clara - Cupertino: 12,983 before 1950, 42,612 before 1960; population_places.csv San Jose 1950, 1970. 100,000 acres: CLAUDE.md pitfall 6. Terrain cover at this zoom (buildings load from 12.5).

title: The Beats
text: A new kind of writer gathers in the cafes of North Beach. On October 7, 1955, Allen Ginsberg first reads his poem “Howl” in public. City Lights, the bookstore here, publishes it; its owner is tried for selling an obscene book and acquitted in 1957.
note: [SF] Not in the repo tables: checked on Wikipedia City_Lights_Bookstore and Six_Gallery_reading (2026-11): City Lights founded 1953 at 261 Columbus Ave (37.7975, -122.4067); Howl first read Oct 7, 1955 at the Six Gallery, 3119 Fillmore St; published by City Lights 1956; trial Aug 16 - Sep 3, 1957, poem found not obscene. Map shows the North Beach blocks (places.csv North Beach label; DataSF footprints).

title: Silicon Comes to the Valley
text: In 1956 William Shockley, co-inventor of the transistor, opens a laboratory in Mountain View to make transistors from silicon. A year later eight of his engineers quit to start Fairchild Semiconductor. Their spin-offs give the region its name: Silicon Valley.
note: [South Bay] Not in the repo tables: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11): lab opened 1956 at 391 San Antonio Road, Mountain View (37.405, -122.111), first silicon-device company in the valley; eight left in 1957 to form Fairchild; name from Don Hoefler's 1971 article. Intel (1968): general knowledge. Map shows the 1950s commercial strip (footprints 1952-63; the lab building itself was replaced, today's buildings on the site date from 2018).

title: The Cold War Valley
text: The valley's first big customer is the military. In 1956 Lockheed opens a plant in Sunnyvale to build nuclear missiles launched from submarines and, in secret, America's first spy satellites. Within a few years it is the largest employer in the valley.
note: [South Bay] industrial_sites lockheed_sunnyvale with footprints dated by the USGS editions (decision 38). Polaris missiles, the Corona satellites, largest employer: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: Redevelopment in the Fillmore
text: On May 28, 1956, the city marks 27 blocks of the Western Addition for clearance. This is the Fillmore, the center of Black life in San Francisco. Victorian houses are bulldozed and about 8,000 people are forced out.
note: [SF] redevelopment_areas.csv wa_a1 (established May 28, 1956; 27 blocks; ~8,000 residents evicted; clearance 1956-1963 ESTIMATED), wa_a2 (1966-1973); Sanborn-traced fabric ends at the clearance. "Center of Black life": general knowledge.

title: A Valley Under Water
text: Monticello Dam, finished in 1957, plugs a narrow canyon east of Napa and drowns the farming town of Monticello to store water for Solano County. Lake Berryessa takes six years to fill. Its spillway is a giant concrete funnel in the lake known as the Glory Hole.
note: [North Bay] landmarks_northbay.csv monticello_dam (built 1953.5-1957.85, with the Glory Hole); water_history: Lake Berryessa dated from the National Inventory of Dams. Town of Monticello, filling by 1963: the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The Freeway Revolt
text: Engineers plan to cross San Francisco with elevated freeways. One of the first, a double-deck road in front of the Ferry Building, opens on February 5, 1959. That January, after years of protest, the city's supervisors had voted to block most of the rest.
note: [SF] events.csv 1959-02-05 Embarcadero Freeway (freeway revolt that January blocked further routes); landmark model embarcadero_freeway (built 1957.5-1959.1, end 1991.3; route LOW CONFIDENCE) / routes.csv fwy_embarcadero.

title: Big-League Baseball Arrives
text: April 15, 1958: the Giants, just moved from New York, beat the Dodgers 8–0 at Seals Stadium in the first major-league game ever played on the West Coast. Two years later the team moves to windy Candlestick Park, and the old ballpark is torn down.
note: [SF] landmarks.csv seals_stadium (1931-1959). The game of April 15, 1958 (Giants 8, Dodgers 0): general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: Frank Lloyd Wright in Marin
text: Marin County hires the 90-year-old architect Frank Lloyd Wright to design its government center. He dies in 1959 before work begins, but his long, arched buildings, bridging three hills under a sky-blue roof, open in 1962. It is his last major work.
note: [North Bay] landmarks_southbay.csv marin_civic_center_admin (1962), marin_civic_center_hall_of_justice (1969). Wright hired 1957, died April 9, 1959: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: A City on the Bay
text: Brewer Island, a diked marsh used as pasture, is raised with 18 million cubic yards of sand dredged from the bay. The first residents of Foster City move in on March 7, 1964. Alarm at projects like this leads the state, in 1965, to take control of bay fill.
note: [Peninsula] fill_zones.csv sm_foster_city_diked (1897-1901), sm_foster_city_fill (1961-1971; 18 million yd3; first residents March 7, 1964); water_history.csv Foster City Lagoon (1963); places.csv smc_foster_city (1964-). State control of bay fill in 1965 (McAteer-Petris Act / BCDC): general knowledge, not in the repo.

title: Little Boxes
text: South of San Francisco, the builder Henry Doelger covers the hills of Daly City with thousands of look-alike pastel houses. Driving past in 1962, folk singer Malvina Reynolds writes "Little Boxes," a song that turns the Westlake district into a symbol of American suburbia.
note: [Peninsula] Region buildings of Westlake, Daly City (years from the San Mateo County data: 1949-1960s). Doelger's Westlake, Reynolds's 1962 song: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: Saving the Coast
text: September 13, 1962: with developers already dividing the peninsula into house lots, President John F. Kennedy signs a law creating Point Reyes National Seashore. Ten years later a second park, the Golden Gate National Recreation Area, protects the headlands on both sides of the Golden Gate.
note: [North Bay] Terrain: Point Reyes stays natural cover; landmarks_southbay.csv point_reyes_lighthouse (1870). Act of September 13, 1962; GGNRA October 27, 1972: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The Free Speech Movement
text: The university at Berkeley has banned political organizing on campus. On October 1, 1964, when police arrest an activist at an information table, thousands of students surround the police car for 32 hours. After a sit-in and nearly 800 arrests, the students win.
note: [East Bay] Map shows Sproul Plaza: known_building_dates_region.csv ucb_sproul_hall (1941-), landmarks_eastbay.csv sather_gate. Not in the repo tables: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11): Oct 1, 1964 arrest of Jack Weinberg, police car surrounded 32 hours by up to 3,000; Sproul Hall sit-in Dec 2, close to 800 arrests Dec 4; rules changed Jan 3, 1965.

title: Ghirardelli Square
text: When the Ghirardelli chocolate company leaves its old brick factory on the waterfront, a shipping heir buys the block to save it from demolition. Reopened in 1964 as shops and restaurants, it is the first big American project to give old industrial buildings a new use.
note: [SF] SF buildings of the block (North Point / Larkin / Beach / Polk; brick factory buildings by their years). William Roth's purchase (1962), reopening in November 1964, first major adaptive reuse: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The Sea Ranch
text: On a sheep ranch on the Sonoma coast, architects try a new kind of development in 1965: plain wooden houses shaped by the wind and sun, set back so the meadows stay open. But it closes off miles of shore, and the fight that follows leads to California's coastal protection law.
note: [North Bay] landmarks_northbay.csv sea_ranch_condominium_one (built 1964.6-1965.8). Public-access fight, Proposition 20 (1972) and the Coastal Act (1976): general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The Container Port
text: Shipping changes: instead of men carrying cargo piece by piece, cranes lift steel boxes from ship to truck. Oakland builds for it, with container service from 1962 and its first big cranes in 1966. San Francisco's old piers cannot adapt, and its port declines.
note: [East Bay] industrial_sites oakland_port_terminals (1962.7-; Sea-Land service from Sept 5, 1962); landmarks_ports.csv oak_sealand_cranes_1966 (built 1965.8-1966.4), oak_sealand_cranes_1968, oak_crane_x421 (1968). San Francisco's decline as a cargo port: general knowledge.

title: Two Miles, Perfectly Straight
text: In 1966 Stanford switches on a particle accelerator two miles long, still the longest of its kind; a freeway is later built across it. Experiments here show that the proton is made of smaller pieces, called quarks. In 1991 the laboratory puts up the first web site in America.
note: [Peninsula] landmarks_southbay.csv slac_klystron_gallery (1966). First beam May 1966; quark experiments 1967-73 (Nobel Prize 1990); first web server outside Europe, December 1991: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: Compton's Cafeteria
text: One night in August 1966, police try to arrest a customer at Compton's Cafeteria in the Tenderloin. Transgender women and drag queens fight back, throwing cups and smashing windows. It is one of the first uprisings for LGBTQ rights in America, three years before New York's Stonewall riots.
note: [SF] SF buildings at Turk and Taylor Streets (101 Taylor St stands from 1908). The riot of August 1966 (exact night unrecorded): the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The Beatles' Last Concert
text: August 29, 1966: on a cold, foggy night the Beatles play eleven songs in about half an hour on a stage near second base at Candlestick Park. Worn out by touring, they have quietly decided this will be the end. They never again perform for a paying audience.
note: [SF] landmarks.csv candlestick_park_1960 (the open stadium, 1960-1971). The concert of August 29, 1966: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The Black Panthers
text: October 1966: Huey Newton and Bobby Seale, who met as students at Merritt College here in North Oakland, found the Black Panther Party. Its members carry guns and follow police patrols to watch for brutality; later they serve free breakfasts to schoolchildren.
note: [East Bay] Not in the repo tables: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11): founded October 1966 in Oakland by Newton and Seale, who met at Merritt College; armed patrols monitoring police; Free Breakfast for Children from January 1969. Location of the old Merritt College campus (Grove St, now Martin Luther King Jr. Way, near 57th St): general knowledge, NOT checked. Map shows the North Oakland blocks beside the SR-24 corridor being cleared (redevelopment_areas.csv oak_sr24_*, 1965-67.5).

title: The Summer of Love
text: On January 14, 1967, some 20,000 to 30,000 people gather in Golden Gate Park for a “Human Be-In.” That summer as many as 100,000 young people come to the Haight-Ashbury neighborhood, drawn by rock music, drugs and the promise of a freer way of life.
note: [SF] events.csv 1967-01-14 Human Be-In (20,000-30,000 at the Polo Fields, 3.5 km west of this view); places.csv sf_haight_ashbury label; map shows the Victorian blocks of the Haight and the Panhandle. "As many as 100,000": checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11).

title: The Mother of All Demos
text: December 9, 1968: at a computer conference in the Civic Center, Douglas Engelbart of the Stanford Research Institute shows a thousand engineers things none of them has seen: a mouse, windows, clickable links, shared documents and video calls. The industry needs twenty years to catch up.
note: [SF] landmarks.csv civic_auditorium (1915); the Fall Joint Computer Conference met there and in Brooks Hall beneath the plaza. Engelbart's 90-minute demonstration: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: People's Park
text: In April 1969 Berkeley students and neighbors turn a vacant university lot into a park. On May 15 the university fences it off. In the clash that follows, police fire shotguns, killing one man, and Governor Ronald Reagan sends the National Guard to occupy the city for two weeks.
note: [East Bay] Berkeley Southside buildings and the cleared block (houses there end in the university's 1967-68 clearance). May 15, 1969 ("Bloody Thursday", James Rector killed): general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The Occupation of Alcatraz
text: November 20, 1969: 89 Native Americans land on Alcatraz, empty since the prison closed, and claim the island for all tribes. They hold it for 19 months. The occupation draws national attention to the treatment of Native Americans.
note: [SF] events.csv 1969-11-20 Occupation of Alcatraz (89 American Indians and supporters, 19 months); landmarks.csv alcatraz_cellhouse, alcatraz_water_tower. "Claim for all tribes" (Indians of All Tribes) and national attention: general knowledge.

title: The Transamerica Pyramid
text: Downtown San Francisco is filling with office towers. The most argued-over is an 853-foot pyramid, built from December 1969 to 1972 where the Montgomery Block stood. It stays the city's tallest building until 2017 and becomes its symbol.
note: [SF] events.csv 1972 Transamerica Pyramid (853 ft, site of the Montgomery Block, tallest until 2017); landmark model transamerica_pyramid (built 1969.95-1972.5), california_555 (1969), embarcadero_center_1 (1971). "Most argued-over": general knowledge.

title: A Restaurant in Berkeley
text: August 28, 1971: Alice Waters, 27, opens Chez Panisse in a wooden house on Shattuck Avenue, serving one set dinner cooked from whatever nearby farms have picked that day. The idea, building meals around fresh local ingredients, changes how Americans eat.
note: [East Bay] Berkeley buildings on Shattuck Ave north of the campus (1517 Shattuck; years from the roll). Opening on August 28, 1971: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: Playland at the Beach
text: For half a century San Franciscans ride the streetcar out to the ocean for Playland's fun house, carousel and midway; the It's-It ice cream sandwich is invented here in 1928. The amusement park closes on September 4, 1972, and apartments take its place.
note: [SF] landmarks.csv playland_fun_house, playland_carousel, playland_midway (to 1972; the Big Dipper coaster to 1955). Closing on September 4, 1972; It's-It (1928): general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: BART
text: The region's answer to traffic is a new electric railway, Bay Area Rapid Transit, or BART. The first trains run on September 11, 1972, between Fremont and Oakland. On September 16, 1974, they start running under the bay itself, through a tube laid on the bottom.
note: [East Bay] transit_openings.csv bart_fremont_macarthur (1972-09-11), bart_transbay (1974-09-16), lines of 1973 in between; events.csv 1974-09-16 BART Under the Bay; trains and stations per decision 24. "Tube laid on the bottom": general knowledge.

title: Pong
text: In 1972 a new company called Atari sets up a coin-operated video game, Pong, in a neighborhood tavern here in Sunnyvale. Within days it stops working, because the coin box has overflowed with quarters. The video game industry grows from that machine.
note: [South Bay] Region building at 157 W El Camino Real, Sunnyvale (then Andy Capp's Tavern; named Rooster T. Feathers in the Overture data). Atari founded June 27, 1972; the prototype's test in the tavern: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The Office of the Future
text: Xerox, the copier company, opens a research center in the Palo Alto hills to invent the office of the future. In the 1970s its scientists build a personal computer with windows, icons and a mouse, plus the laser printer and Ethernet. Xerox sells few of them; Apple and others borrow the ideas.
note: [Peninsula] Region building at 3333 Coyote Hill Road (dated 1974-75 in the data). PARC founded 1970, the Alto (1973), laser printer, Ethernet, Steve Jobs's 1979 visit: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: Two Steves and a Garage
text: March 5, 1975: hobbyists who want computers of their own form the Homebrew Computer Club in a Menlo Park garage. One of them, Steve Wozniak, designs a small computer; his friend Steve Jobs sees a business. They start Apple in 1976 in the Jobs family home here.
note: [South Bay] Not in the repo tables: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11): first meeting March 5, 1975 in Gordon French's garage, Menlo Park; Wozniak designed the Apple I after it. Apple's founding in 1976 at the Jobs home, 2066 Crist Drive, Los Altos (37.3403, -122.0689): general knowledge, NOT checked. Map shows the 1950s tract houses of the street (footprints 1950-53).

title: The Judgment of Paris
text: May 24, 1976: at a blind tasting in Paris, French judges rank a Chardonnay from Chateau Montelena, this stone winery near Calistoga, and a Napa Cabernet above the best wines of France. The upset makes Napa Valley famous and its vineyards some of the costliest farmland in America.
note: [North Bay] Region building Chateau Montelena Winery (named in the Overture data; stone winery of 1888) and the valley's vineyard cover. The tasting of May 24, 1976 (1973 Chateau Montelena Chardonnay, 1973 Stag's Leap Wine Cellars Cabernet): general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The Last Waltz
text: Winterland, an old ice rink, is promoter Bill Graham's biggest rock hall; the Grateful Dead, Jimi Hendrix and Led Zeppelin all play here. On Thanksgiving night, November 25, 1976, the Band gives its farewell concert, filmed by Martin Scorsese as "The Last Waltz."
note: [SF] notable_demolished.csv winterland_1928 (1928-1985, Post and Steiner Streets). The concert of November 25, 1976: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The I-Hotel
text: The International Hotel is the last piece of Manilatown, home to elderly Filipino and Chinese men who came to America as laborers decades earlier. Its owner wants a parking garage. On August 4, 1977, 400 police push through a human chain of 3,000 protesters and evict the tenants.
note: [SF] notable_demolished.csv international_hotel_1907 (848 Kearny St at Jackson, 1907-1981). The eviction of August 4, 1977: the cited Wikipedia page.

title: Harvey Milk
text: By the 1970s the Castro is the center of gay life in San Francisco. Harvey Milk, who runs a camera shop on this street, is elected to the city's Board of Supervisors on November 8, 1977: the first openly gay man elected to public office in California.
note: [SF] Map shows Castro Street with landmarks.csv castro_theatre (1922-) and the places.csv The Castro label (1970-). Not in the repo tables: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11): Castro Camera opened on Castro Street in March 1973; elected Nov 8, 1977; first openly gay man elected to public office in California.

title: Biotechnology Is Born
text: In 1976 a young investor and a San Francisco biochemist, Herbert Boyer, start a company to make medicines by splicing human genes into bacteria. Genentech moves into a warehouse here in South San Francisco in 1978 and that year produces human insulin. An industry grows up around it.
note: [Peninsula] Region buildings on Point San Bruno, South San Francisco (the first dated 1978 in the data). Founded April 7, 1976 by Robert Swanson and Herbert Boyer; synthetic human insulin 1978: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The Rainbow Flag
text: June 25, 1978: two huge flags with eight colored stripes fly over United Nations Plaza for the Gay Freedom Day parade. The artist Gilbert Baker and 30 volunteers have dyed and sewn them by hand, urged on by Harvey Milk. The rainbow flag becomes a symbol of gay pride around the world.
note: [SF] SF Civic Center buildings round United Nations Plaza (Market St at Hyde). First flown June 25, 1978: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: November 27, 1978
text: Mayor George Moscone and Supervisor Harvey Milk are shot dead in City Hall by Dan White, a former supervisor. That night thousands carry candles from the Castro to City Hall. Nine days earlier, over 900 members of a San Francisco church had died at Jonestown, Guyana.
note: [SF] events.csv 1978-11-27 Moscone and Milk Killed (in City Hall, by former supervisor Dan White); landmarks.csv city_hall_1915. Candlelight march and Jonestown (November 18, 1978): general knowledge, NOT checked.

title: The Catch
text: January 10, 1982, Candlestick Park: with 58 seconds left, Joe Montana throws to Dwight Clark, who leaps to catch the ball at the back of the end zone. The San Francisco 49ers beat Dallas 28–27 and go on to win their first Super Bowl.
note: [SF] Map shows landmarks.csv candlestick_park_1971 (enclosed stadium, 1971-2015; opened 1960 on fill, fill_zones sf_candlestick_park). The game: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11), not in the repo.

title: The AIDS Epidemic
text: In 1981 doctors begin seeing young gay men dying of an illness no one understands. San Francisco is among the cities hit hardest. In 1983 San Francisco General Hospital opens Ward 5B, the first hospital ward in the country just for AIDS patients.
note: [SF] Map shows the hospital: known_building_dates.csv sfgh_1915_wards, zsfg_building_5 (1976). WEAKLY CHECKED: Wikipedia (5B film page) calls Ward 5B at San Francisco General, 1983, the first AIDS ward in the United States; the hospital page says its Ward 86 was instrumental in early AIDS care. The month (July 1983), the 1981 first cases and "hit hardest" are general knowledge.

title: Wind Power at Altamont
text: After the oil shocks of the 1970s, California offers tax breaks for wind power. Beginning in 1981, thousands of small turbines go up on the windy hills of Altamont Pass, for years the largest wind farm in the world. Most have since been replaced by a few hundred giant ones.
note: [East Bay] landmarks_coastsouth.csv altamont_patterson_pass_1985 (survivors of two 1985 projects) and the later repowered farms (2004-2021) at their US Wind Turbine Database positions. First turbines 1981, once the world's largest wind farm: the cited Wikipedia page.

title: Burning Man
text: June 22, 1986: on the summer solstice, Larry Harvey and a friend carry an eight-foot wooden figure of a man down to Baker Beach and set it on fire, and a small crowd gathers to watch. They repeat it every year until 1990, when the growing event moves to the Nevada desert.
note: [SF] Terrain: Baker Beach below the Presidio. The first burn on June 22, 1986 (Larry Harvey and Jerry James): general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: A Birthday on the Bridge
text: May 24, 1987: for the Golden Gate Bridge's 50th birthday the roadway is closed to cars and opened to walkers. About 300,000 people crowd onto it at once, and their weight flattens the gentle arch of the deck. The bridge holds.
note: [SF] landmarks.csv golden_gate_bridge. Not in the repo tables: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11): May 24, 1987, closed to cars, roughly 300,000 people on the bridge, center span flattened. No crowd is drawn.

title: The Loma Prieta Earthquake
text: October 17, 1989, 5:04 p.m.: a magnitude 6.9 earthquake strikes. In West Oakland the upper deck of a double-deck freeway, the Cypress Viaduct, falls onto the lower one, killing 42 people. A section of the Bay Bridge's deck collapses too.
note: [East Bay] routes.csv fwy_cypress (1957.44-1989.79; collapsed Oct 17, 1989, 42 deaths); events.csv 1989-10-17 Loma Prieta Earthquake (magnitude 6.9, 5:04 p.m., Bay Bridge deck section).

title: Santa Cruz, 1989
text: The earthquake is centered in the mountains ten miles from Santa Cruz. The old brick buildings of its main street, Pacific Avenue, crumble, and three people die there. The Cooper House of 1895 and the Hotel Metropole are among the buildings lost.
note: [Santa Cruz] notable_demolished_region.csv scz_cooper_house_1895 (-1989.82), scz_hotel_metropole_1908 (-1989.88), scz_st_george_hotel_1895 (-1990). Epicenter about 10 miles northeast of Santa Cruz and three deaths on the Pacific Garden Mall: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11), not in the repo.

title: The Freeway Comes Down
text: In San Francisco the quake does its worst damage in the Marina District, built on the fill of 1912, and it cracks the Embarcadero Freeway. Instead of repairing it, the city tears it down, starting February 27, 1991, and the waterfront opens up again.
note: [SF] events.csv 1991-02-27 The Freeway Comes Down, 1989-10-17 (Marina District buildings burn and collapse); landmark model embarcadero_freeway ends 1991.3; fill_zones.csv sf_marina_cove_1912 (liquefied in 1989).

title: The Oakland Hills Firestorm
text: October 20, 1991: a fire in the hills above Oakland, driven by hot, dry wind, races through neighborhoods of wooden houses among the trees. It burns 1,520 acres, kills 25 people and destroys 2,843 houses and 437 apartments.
note: [East Bay] Fire-only stop: events.csv 1991-10-20 Oakland Hills Firestorm (1,520 acres, 25 dead, 2,843 houses and 437 apartment and condominium units); redevelopment_areas.csv fire_tunnel_1991 (clearance 1991.8, FRAP perimeter).

title: The Army Leaves the Presidio
text: October 1, 1994: after 218 years as a military post under Spain, Mexico and the United States, the Presidio is handed to the National Park Service. Its barracks and hospitals become homes, offices and museums, set in a forest on some of the most valuable land in America.
note: [SF] Presidio buildings by their researched years (known_building_dates.csv), landmarks.csv presidio_forest (planted from 1886). Transfer on October 1, 1994: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The Web Goes Public
text: August 9, 1995: Netscape, a 16-month-old Mountain View company whose browser has made the World Wide Web easy to use, sells its stock to the public. The price more than doubles on the first day, though the company has never made a profit. The dot-com boom has begun.
note: [South Bay] Region buildings at 501 E Middlefield Road, Mountain View (1988-93 in the data). Founded April 4, 1994; IPO August 9, 1995: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: A Ballpark on the Bay
text: March 31, 2000: baseball's Giants leave windy Candlestick Park for a new ballpark on old railroad land at China Basin. It is the first major-league ballpark built without public money since 1962, and the first piece of a rebuilt southern waterfront.
note: [SF] events.csv 2000-03-31 Pac Bell Park Opens (first MLB park built without public funds since 1962); landmark model oracle_park (built 1997.95-2000.25); redevelopment_areas.csv mission_bay (rail yards cleared from 1998).

title: Google
text: The internet sets off a new boom. On September 4, 1998, two Stanford students, Larry Page and Sergey Brin, found a search company called Google in a friend's garage in Menlo Park. In 2003 it moves into this Mountain View campus, built for an older computer maker.
note: [South Bay] landmarks_southbay.csv googleplex_sgi_campus (built 1994.5-1997.5 for Silicon Graphics; leased by Google from 2003, bought June 2006 for $319 million). Founding on September 4, 1998 in Susan Wojcicki's garage, Menlo Park: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11).

title: The Dot-Com Bubble
text: By 2000, hundreds of internet startups have crowded into the old warehouses around South Park, and rents have soared. Technology stocks peak on March 10, 2000, then lose most of their value. Within two years many of the companies are gone and their offices stand empty.
note: [SF] SF buildings round South Park (brick warehouses of 1909-13 and later infill). Nasdaq peak on March 10, 2000; the collapse of 2000-02: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: Pixar
text: In 1995 a small studio in Point Richmond releases "Toy Story," the first feature film animated entirely by computer. With the money from its hits, Pixar builds this campus on the site of an old cannery in Emeryville and moves in at the end of 2000.
note: [East Bay] Region buildings of the Pixar campus, 1200 Park Avenue, Emeryville (2000-01 in the data). Toy Story (November 22, 1995); the Emeryville campus on the former Del Monte cannery site: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: Weddings at City Hall
text: February 12, 2004: Mayor Gavin Newsom orders the city to issue marriage licenses to same-sex couples. About 4,000 couples receive them in a month before the courts call a halt and void the marriages. Same-sex marriage becomes legal nationwide in 2015.
note: [SF] landmarks.csv city_hall_1915. Not in the repo tables: checked on the cited Wikipedia page (2026-11): licenses from Feb 12, 2004, about 4,000 before the halt of March 11, voided Aug 12, 2004. Nationwide legality in 2015: general knowledge.

title: The iPhone
text: January 9, 2007: on stage at the Moscone West convention hall, Apple's Steve Jobs holds up a phone with no keyboard, only a touch screen. "Today, Apple is going to reinvent the phone," he says. Within a few years most people carry a computer in their pocket.
note: [SF] SF building Moscone West (2003, Fourth and Howard Streets). Macworld keynote of January 9, 2007: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: A New East Span
text: The 1989 earthquake showed that the eastern half of the Bay Bridge could fail. Its replacement, a single-tower suspension bridge and a long viaduct, opens on September 2, 2013. The old steel span beside it is taken apart piece by piece and is gone by 2017.
note: [East Bay] events.csv 2013-09-02 New Bay Bridge Span; landmark models bay_bridge_east_2013_sas (built 2009.0-2013.67), _skyway, bay_bridge_east_1936_cantilever (end 2015.45), _trusses (2016.6), _causeway (2017.2). Camera point = SAS tower, over water (bridge).

title: Electric Cars from Fremont
text: General Motors builds cars at this Fremont plant from 1962, later together with Toyota, until it closes in 2010. That year a small maker of electric cars, Tesla, buys the empty factory for $42 million. By the 2020s it turns out more than half a million cars a year.
note: [East Bay] Region building "Tesla Fremont Factory Body/General Assembly" (named in the Overture data). GM Fremont Assembly 1962-82, NUMMI 1984-2010, Tesla's purchase (May 2010) and opening (October 27, 2010): general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: The Social Network
text: Facebook, started in a Harvard dormitory in 2004, moves to Palo Alto within months and outgrows one office after another. In December 2011 it takes over this campus on the bay shore in Menlo Park, built for an older computer maker. A year later a billion people are using it.
note: [Peninsula] Region buildings at 1 Hacker Way, Menlo Park (built 1995-96 for Sun Microsystems) and Meta MPK 20 / 21 across the expressway (2015, 2018). Move in December 2011; one billion users in October 2012: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: Tech Moves to the City
text: A tax break brings Twitter to a run-down stretch of Market Street in 2012, and technology companies that once kept to the suburbs pour into San Francisco. Rents jump. In December 2013 protesters in the Mission block a private bus carrying Google workers, a symbol of who can afford to stay.
note: [SF] SF buildings of mid-Market (1355 Market St, the 1937 Furniture Mart, Twitter's headquarters from June 2012). Mid-Market payroll tax break (2011); bus blockade of December 9, 2013 at 24th and Valencia: general knowledge / the cited Wikipedia page.

title: Apple Park
text: The valley of orchards is now home to some of the world's largest companies. On land that was fruit trees and then a Hewlett-Packard campus, Apple builds a ring-shaped headquarters 1,512 feet across. Employees move in from April 2017.
note: [South Bay] landmarks_southbay.csv apple_park_ring (construction 2013.9-2017.3; 1,512 ft diameter, 4,805 ft around); vanished_sites hp_cupertino (1969-2014); agriculture.geojson topo_1940s orchard at the site.

title: Salesforce Tower
text: A second tech boom, centered in San Francisco itself, fills the blocks south of Market Street with towers. Salesforce Tower, 1,070 feet and 61 floors, opens on January 8, 2018, as the city's tallest building, beside a new transit terminal with a park on its roof.
